facts.fact_text: The applicant is a political activist.
The applicant is an opposition leader.
The applicant is an anti-corruption campaigner.
The applicant is a popular blogger.
Five applications before the Court concern the applicant's arrests on seven occasions at different public events.
On 5 March 2012 the applicant took part in a meeting at Pushkinskaya Square, Moscow.
The meeting at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 had been called to protest against the allegedly rigged presidential elections in Russia.
The informal consultations at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 began at about 9.30 p.m.
The informal consultations at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 were attended by some 500 people.
According to the applicant, he stayed among others at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 for a meeting with State Duma deputy Mr P.
According to the applicant, those remaining at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 remained peacefully within the pedestrian area of the square and did not obstruct the traffic or access.
According to the Government, the applicant was holding an irregular gathering at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 without prior notification and was shouting political slogans.
At 10.45 p.m. on 5 March 2012 the police arrived at Pushkinskaya Square and arrested the applicant, among many others.
The administrative offence report drawn up on 5 March 2012 stated that the applicant had taken part in an irregular public gathering.
The administrative offence report drawn up on 5 March 2012 stated that the applicant had ignored police orders to disperse.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events of 5 March 2012.
On 8 May 2012 the applicant took part in an overnight 'walkabout', an informal gathering whereby activists peacefully met at a public venue to discuss current affairs.
On 8 May 2012 several dozen activists met up to discuss the inauguration of Mr Vladimir Putin as President of Russia on the previous day (7 May 2012).
At 4.30 a.m. on 8 May 2012, according to the applicant, the applicant was walking down Lubyanskiy Proyezd accompanied by about 170 people.
At 4 a.m. on 8 May 2012, according to the Government, the applicant was walking down Lubyanskiy Proyezd accompanied by about 170 people.
On 8 May 2012 the group walking down Lubyanskiy Proyezd stopped on the stairs of a public building for a group photograph.
On 8 May 2012, while the applicant was taking a group photograph on the stairs of a public building on Lubyanskiy Proyezd, he was arrested by riot police.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Lubyanskiy Proyezd on 8 May 2012.
The applicant was released at 10.50 a.m. on 8 May 2012 following his first arrest that day.
At 11.55 p.m. on 8 May 2012, according to the Government, the applicant was walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street in a cluster of about fifty people.
At 11 p.m. on 8 May 2012, according to the applicant, the applicant was walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street in a cluster of about fifty people.
According to the applicant, the group walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street on 8 May 2012 stayed on the pavement, had no banners or sound equipment, and were causing no nuisance.
On 8 May 2012 on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street the group was surrounded by riot police and the applicant was arrested without any order or warning.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 (2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street on 8 May 2012.
On 9 May 2012 the applicant arrived at 5 a.m. at Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow to take part in an informal meeting with a State Duma deputy.
On 9 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow to attend the Victory Day celebrations.
On 9 May 2012 at Kudrinskaya Square the applicant was among 50 to 100 people peacefully 'walking about' and discussing current affairs.
According to the applicant, the gathering at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 was not a demonstration: there had been no banners and no noise, and no one was chanting slogans or giving speeches.
At 6 a.m. on 9 May 2012 riot police arrived at Kudrinskaya Square and arrested the applicant without issuing any orders or warning.
The three eyewitnesses testified that no one at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 had chanted slogans or made noise or obstructed traffic.
The three eyewitnesses testified that the police had not issued any orders or warnings before arresting the applicant at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012.

On the basis of the written statements of two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow established that the applicant had taken part in an irregular public meeting at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 and had disobeyed a lawful order from the police to disperse.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow found that the applicant had chanted the slogans 'Russia without Putin!' and 'Putin is a thief!' at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow found that the applicant had refused to leave Kudrinskaya Square, which needed to be cleared for the Victory Day celebrations.
On 27 October 2012 the applicant held a static demonstration ('picket', пикетирование) at Lubyanskaya Square in Moscow.

The static demonstration at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012 was part of a series of peaceful pickets held in Moscow in front of the buildings housing the Federal Security Service and the Russian Investigation Committee to protest 'against repressions and torture'.

According to the applicant, his demonstration at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012 was a solo picket (одиночное пикетирование) which was not subject to a prior notification to the competent public authority.
In total, about thirty people consecutively took part in the picket event at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012.
At 3.30 p.m. on 27 October 2012 the police arrested the applicant at 9 Maroseyka Street when he was walking down the street accompanied by a group of people.

According to the applicant, at the moment of his arrest on 27 October 2012 he had finished picketing and was peacefully walking along the pavement; he was not chanting or carrying any banners, but was being followed by a group of people, including journalists, whose number he estimated as 'two dozen'.
According to the Government, the applicant had organised an irregular march on 27 October 2012 without prior notification.
The applicant was taken to the police station at 4.10 p.m. on 27 October 2012.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events of 27 October 2012.

The three eyewitnesses examined at the applicant's request testified that after ending his picket on 27 October 2012, the applicant had walked down the street while speaking with a fellow activist, surrounded by journalists; he remained on the pavement, did not chant slogans, and carried no banners.
The three eyewitnesses testified that several other participants in the picket on 27 October 2012 remained standing with their banners, at a certain distance from each other.
The three eyewitnesses testified that the police arrested the applicant on 27 October 2012 without any warning or explanation.

On the basis of written reports by two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that the applicant had organised and led a group of thirty people on 27 October 2012, thus holding a march without the approval of the local authorities.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that the group on 27 October 2012 was heading from Lubyanskaya Square to Lefortovo detention facility.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that at 9 Maroseyka Street on 27 October 2012 the group had obstructed the road, thus halting traffic.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District found the applicant guilty of taking part in a march which had not been duly notified to the authorities on 27 October 2012.

On 24 February 2014 at 12 noon the applicant went to the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow to attend a hearing involving activists who were on trial for participation in mass disorders at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012.
The judgment in the Bolotnaya Square mass disorders case was to be delivered at a public hearing on 24 February 2014.
On 24 February 2014 the court-house of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow was cordoned off and obstructed by police vans, and the applicant was unable to enter.
On 24 February 2014 the applicant remained outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow among other members of the public wishing to attend the hearing.

According to the applicant, on 24 February 2014 he was standing silently outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow when the police suddenly rushed into the crowd and arrested him, without any order, warning or pretext.
According to the official version, on 24 February 2014 outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow the applicant was holding an irregular gathering and chanting political slogans.
At 12.50 p.m. on 24 February 2014 the applicant was taken to a police station following his first arrest that day.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014.
At about 7.45 p.m. on 24 February 2014 the applicant took part in a peaceful public gathering following the delivery of the judgment in respect of mass disorders at Bolotnaya Square.
The gathering on 24 February 2014 at about 7.45 p.m. had about 150 participants and took place at Tverskaya Street.
On 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street the applicant was arrested while he was standing on the pavement talking to a journalist.
According to the applicant, he had received no order or warning before his second arrest on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street, and he did not resist the police.

According to the police report, when the applicant was being seated in the police vehicle on 24 February 2014 he was waving at the crowd and trying to attract media attention, thus demonstrating a refusal to comply with the police order and resisting the officers in the performance of their duties.

The applicant was charged with disobeying a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.

The two eyewitnesses at the hearing on 25 February 2014 testified that the police had not given the applicant any orders or warnings before proceeding to arrest him at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.
The Tverskoy District Court admitted and examined the video recording of the contested events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.
The Tverskoy District Court questioned the two police officers on whose reports the charges arising from the events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014 were based.
The Tverskoy District Court established that the applicant had taken part in an irregular meeting at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014 and had disobeyed the lawful order of the police to disperse.

On 7 March 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court examined the charges relating to the applicant's alleged participation on 24 February 2014 in an unauthorised public gathering in front of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
The applicant requested that two eyewitnesses present at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014 be examined at the hearing on 7 March 2014.

The applicant requested that the two policemen on whose reports the charges arising from the events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014 were based be examined at the hearing on 7 March 2014.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court dismissed the applicant's requests for examination of two eyewitnesses and two policemen at the hearing on 7 March 2014.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court admitted a video recording of the contested events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014, but decided not to take cognisance of its contents because it was undated and because it had not reproduced the full sequence of events.

On the basis of the written reports by two police officers, the judge of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court found the applicant guilty of taking part in a meeting on 24 February 2014 which had not been notified to the competent authority in accordance with the procedure provided by law.

The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), Section 2, defines a public event as an open, peaceful action accessible to all, held in the form of a gathering, a meeting, a demonstration, a march, or a picket or in various combinations of these forms, organised at the initiative of citizens of the Russian Federation, political parties, other public associations, or religious associations, including events held with the use of vehicles.

The Public Events Act, Section 5 § 4, provides that the organiser of a public event must notify the executive or municipal authority of the public event in accordance with Section 7 of the Public Events Act.

The Public Events Act, Section 7, provides that notification of a public event (except for a gathering and a picket held by a solo participant) must be filed in writing by its organiser with the executive or municipal authority no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days before the date of the public event.

The Public Events Act, Section 16, provides that the grounds for ending a public event include: the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons; commission by the participants of unlawful acts or a deliberate breach by the organiser of the requirements on the procedure for the conduct of public events; and (following legislative amendments of 8 June 2012) non-compliance by the organisers with the obligations set out in Section 5 § 4 of the Public Events Act.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 4, provides that failure to obey lawful orders from police officers or resistance to them by certain participants of the public event may incur liability as provided for by law.

Article 55 § 3 of the Russian Constitution provides that the rights and freedoms of individuals and citizens may be limited by federal law only to the extent required for the protection of the fundamental principles of the constitutional system, morality, health, the rights and lawful interests of other people, and for ensuring the defence of the country and the security of the State.

The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), Section 2, defines a public event as an open, peaceful action accessible to all, held in the form of a gathering, a meeting, a demonstration, a march, or a picket or in various combinations of these forms, organised at the initiative of citizens of the Russian Federation, political parties, other public associations, or religious associations, including events held with the use of vehicles.

The Public Events Act, Section 2, provides that the aim of a public event is the free expression and formation of opinions, and to put forward demands on issues of political, economic, social and cultural life in the country, as well as issues of foreign policy.

The Public Events Act, Section 16, provides that the grounds for ending a public event include: the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons; commission by the participants of unlawful acts or a deliberate breach by the organiser of the requirements on the procedure for the conduct of public events; and (following legislative amendments of 8 June 2012) non-compliance by the organisers with the obligations set out in Section 5 § 4 of the Public Events Act.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 1, provides that if it is decided to end the public event, the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall give an order to the organiser to end the public event, having explained the reasons for its termination, and within twenty-four hours shall issue this order in writing and serve it on the organiser; shall set the time for compliance with the order; and if the organiser does not comply, shall directly address the participants and set an additional time for compliance.
The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 2, provides that in the event of non-compliance with the order to end the public event, the police shall take the necessary measures to end the public event.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 3, provides that the procedure for ending a public event set out in Section 17 § 1 shall not apply in the event of mass disorder, mob violence, arson, or other situations requiring urgent action.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 4, provides that failure to obey lawful orders from police officers or resistance to them by certain participants of the public event may incur liability as provided for by law.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that according to international standards, if the domestic legal framework foresees a notification procedure, its objective should be to allow State authorities the opportunity to facilitate the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly, and that failure to notify the authorities of an assembly does not render it unlawful and should not be used as a basis for dispersing it.
